utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honour, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Laurie Sartorio for the Prosecution assisted by our intern Laura Greer and our case manager Alma Imamovic-Ivanov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution's office, to everyone in and around the courtroom. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and I appear together with Nicholas Robson on behalf of General Delic. With us is Lejla Gluhic our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you please stand up. Would you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic, I guess that's your witness. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karahasanovic. Could you please give your full name to the Tribunal for the record?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is Izet Karahasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What is your date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of March, 1958, in Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what do you do for a living now?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed education as a wood processing technician. I work in the Krivaja factory as a foreman, and I supervise some 25 works.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can take you to the start of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when the war started, did you join any military unit?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, towards the end of that year when the first conflicts broke out in Slovenia at first and then in Croatia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina there were incidents taking place. In Zavidovici, we founded the Patriotic League. In my village, I formed a platoon comprising 30 volunteers. We stood guard in our village. We were not particularly well armed. We had a few hunting rifles and maybe two handguns.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And prior to you forming a platoon in your village, did you have any military experience?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed my military service term with the JNA in 1979. I was a plain soldier with the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And how long were you in the JNA for?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you remain within the platoon in your village or did you join any other unit?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war broke out, my platoon joined the Kovaci Battalion which is a municipality, or rather, like a commune within the municipality of Zavidovici. The battalion was formed out of certain plans; however, not all of them in the area joined the platoon -- joined the battalion. But at that time, the Patriotic League ceased to exist and the TO had been formed. There were, however, platoons, as I said, which remained independent of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us approximately when it was that you joined the Kovaci battalion?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, in April 1992, that's when the war officially began in Bosnia and Herzegovina and we joined the Kovaci battalion. I remained in command of my platoon within the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did you remain a member of the Kovaci battalion throughout the war, or did you become a member of any other unit?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another transformation, so to say, the TO ceased to exist and brigades were formed. With my battalion, I became a member of the 318th Brigade in Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you say approximately when you became a member of the 318th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1992 and early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did you remain within the 318th Brigade or were there any other further changes?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our battalion remained within the brigade for a while and then there was another change. Two brigades were formed within the municipality of Zavidovici, the 318th and the 320th. We remained part of the 320th Brigade from that point onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did you serve in the 320th Brigade until the end of the war, or, again, were there further changes?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later, in 1994, towards the end, the two brigades were merged into one again, becoming the 328th Brigade. I remained with that brigade. However, I was no longer platoon commander, but I became company commander within the 320th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you remain in that position -- sorry, if we could just clarify your last answer. You became the company commander of which brigade, did you say?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became company commander in the 318th Brigade. I forgot to mention that. When it became the 328th Brigade, I was appointed assistant commander for security of the 328th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And which unit did you become the assistant commander for security of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm getting confused here. Sorry, sorry, sorry. I'm getting confused.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm getting confused, Mr. Robson. The witness says at page 4, starting from line 13: "Our battalion within the brigade for a while, and then there was another change. Two brigades were formed within the municipality of Zavidovici, the 318th and the 320th. We remained part of the 320th Brigade from that point onwards." Now, at that same page, at line 21 to 22, he says: "However, I was no longer platoon commander, but I became company commander within the 320th." Then you asked him to explain, and your next question was: "Did you remain in that position -- sorry, if we could just clarify your last answer." He says: "I became company commander in the 318th Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness just to clarify the sequence of brigades that he was a member of, if he can just tell us chronologically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He has just told us that when the 318th and the 320th were formed, he stayed in the 320th. Now suddenly he becomes a commander in the 318th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karahasanovic, can you clarify this for us?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I failed to describe the exact developments. When I became commander in 1993, that was with the 318th Brigade. I became [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosnian Muslim"] company commander there, since I only commanded the platoon for a year. Therefore, I became company commander in the 318th. Later on, another brigade was formed within the Zavidovici municipality. Our battalion was then made part of the 320th Brigade. I remained company commander within the 320th. Then the two brigades merged again into one, being the 328th, where I was promoted to assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Again, I'm getting confused. He says: "When I became commander in 1993, that was with the 318th Brigade." Now, I don't understand what is written here says: "Bosnian Muslim company commander." I am not sure whether I heard him say that. "Therefore I became company commander in the 318th. Later on, another brigade was formed within the Zavidovici municipality." He doesn't tell us what is the name of that brigade. But then he says: "Our battalion was then made part of the 320th Brigade." What is the other brigade that was formed? Is it the 320th that you were made a part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, 318th and 320th then merged into one, called 320th, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 328th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, the 318th and 320th merged into one to become 328th; is that what you are saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That explains it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And which unit of the 328th Brigade did you become the assistant commander for security of?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 4th Battalion of the 328th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When you became the assistant commander for security, did you have any previous experience that enabled you to carry out your role as a security officer?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those of us who were appointed officers in battalions had no experience. They simply assessed our readiness and level of education. We did not undergo any special preparation or training. We simply worked of our own accord as best we knew how. It was war, and there was no time for us to educate ourselves any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you remain the assistant commander for security of the 4th Battalion of the 328th Brigade, or were there any further changes to your position?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995, there were changes. At the level of assistance [Realtime transcript read in error "civilian"] commanders for security, I was transferred from the 4th Battalion to the 5th Battalion; whereas, my colleague from the 5th Battalion was transferred to the 4th. All battalions were included, and all of them saw changes in terms of different people being appointed assistant commanders for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the first part of your answer Mr. Karahasanovic. At which level was it that you say that you were transferred from the 4th Battalion to the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of assistant commanders for security. I have to clarify. Since we worked in the environment where people knew each other and officers knew each other, the changes were made because people were getting too close to each other. That's why assistant commanders for security were being transferred, and I switched positions with the colleague from the 5th Battalion. They knew they were moving us to a unit where we didn't know other people, and they thought we would function better in a such an environment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Any transcription errors will be corrected later, pertaining to the repetition of the last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karahasanovic, do you remember when you became the assistant commander for security in the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion, I believe it was early September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you assumed that position in the 5th Battalion, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander of the 5th Battalion was Sehic Ahmed. Within the 328th Mountain Brigade, it was Enes Malcibegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if I can clarify, the commander of your unit, the 5th Battalion, was Ahmed Sehic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what position within the 328th Mountain Brigade did Enes Malcibegovic hold?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assistant commander for security of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened in September 1995 when you joined the 5th Battalion, briefly?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed assistant commander for security in a unit I did not know, then I became acquainting myself with the officers at the level of battalions, assistant commanders, company commanders, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you describe for us briefly what your main duties were at that time?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My basic and main duty, as assistant commander for security in the 5th Mountain Battalion, was to take care of security of officers, soldiers, materiel, and equipment, as well as monitor any distribution of food, cigarettes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And at that point in time, September 1995, did the 5th Battalion have a command?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 5th Battalion did have a battalion command three kilometres done the Gostovic river, since all battalion members lived in the area around Gostovici. They were transferred down the Krivij river. Before I arrived in the battalion, they had formed a forward command post that was in Polje, down the Krivij some 12 kilometres away from Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, just to clarify, the 5th Battalion had its main command post three kilometres south of Zavidovici?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it had a forward command post in the field at Polje. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Polje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And were its members based at any other locations apart from those two places?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. The lines were far from Polje, the lines of Defence, that is. There was another IKM in Marici, but usually there would be only one officer there as well as company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did any combat action take place during the month of September 1995?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived in the 5th Battalion, I think it was the 10th of September, there was combat to liberate Vozuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can ask you about the activities that day on the 10th of September. Can you explain for us what happened?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, early in the morning, I was still sleeping at Polje at the IKM. I had an office there with a bed. I would spend two to three days there on occasion, and then I would go home for a day or two. That morning, however, I was asleep in Polje, and I heard firing along the entire defence line which meant that combat had started. As I was having breakfast with several other officers, we decided to leave for Marici to the IKM there; and around noon, at Marici we were told to go to the defence line to observe further developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go into the events that day in a little more detail in a moment. But before we do so, let me ask you this: Prior to these combat activities on the 10th of September, had you ever been involved in the capture of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never had any captured persons, and I had no contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you know what, if anything, the members of the 328th Brigade were supposed to do in the event that they captured prisoners of war during a combat action?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At meetings held at the level of brigade, with assistant commanders for security, we were told what we were supposed to do with prisoners. We were advised how to treat them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what were you told to do in relation to prisoners; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that, in case we have POWs, first we had to search them and remove any weapons or similar objects. They should also be taken their IDs and their first and last names as well as dates of birth noted down. The brigade should then be informed so that they could dispatch the military police, since our battalion did not have its own military policemen. Such military policemen were supposed to take them to the brigade where statements were supposed to be taken from those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now like to return back to the events on the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And at this stage, Your Honours, if we could please bring up map number 12 from the map collection. I will be asking the witness to make some markings on this map as well. If we could close in on the left-hand side of the map, upper left-hand side, please. I think we can probably close in a little further as well. Is it possible to move across to the right-hand side, keeping the map at the same scale? Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this number 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it differs from the map that I've got here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's map number 12 we're after. The ERN number is 06186707. That's better. And, again, if we could please close up, and if we can scroll down, please. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karahasanovic, are you able to make out the names of the places on this map? I'm not asking you to read them, but are you able to see what they say?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You told us that you were at Polje on the morning of the 10th of September. Do you see where Polje is on the map?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you able to draw a circle around Polje and mark it with a number 1?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You then told us that you went -- well, you've mentioned, at Marici, there was another forward command post. Do you see Marici on this map?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see Marici. It doesn't say Marici anywhere on this map, but I know approximately where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you able to draw a circle around the location where Marici is and to mark it with a number 2?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So turning to the events on the 10th of September, did you go through Marici after leaving Polje that day?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We stopped at Marici for a while and then we continued on. We went there by car because it's quite a distance. It would have taken us a long time to walk there, so we drove to Marici; and then from Marici, I and two other men went to our position at the defence line. That was our defence line, because the fighting was already under way and our unit was supposed to clear up the terrain following after the units that had liberated this area, and our lines were not manned anymore. We were supposed to be there at one segment of the line where there was a phone, and we were supposed to be there to observe further work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did the location at the defence line that you went to have a name?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Malovan, Malovan Greda.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Again, could you draw a circle around the location that you went to with the defence line and mark that with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what happened once you got to Malovan Greda?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we sat down there in a dugout until our unit, that was the 2nd Mountain Company, descended down Malovan Greda moving down Kesten; and then in the afternoon, I got a call from the company commander, Ismet Sogan [as interpreted], who told me that he had some enemy soldiers that had been captured. He told me that he had some captive soldiers and that this was something for me, that I was supposed to go there and see what should be done with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you repeat for us the name of the officer that called you on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ismet Sogolj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if you can just spell the name of Mr. Sogolj?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: S-O-G-O-L-J.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what was his position, just so we're clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. If I may just interrupt you, now that we've made corrections. You said, sir, you descended down Malovan Greda, moving down to where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The unit moved down Malovan Greda; and throughout that time, I was at Malovan Greda up until the time when Ismet Sogolj called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What position did Mr. Sogolj hold?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sogolj was the commander of the 2nd Company in the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did he say where he was when he made this call to you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that the prisoners that he had, that he put them in the community hall, that was the biggest facility in Kesten, the place where he could actually put they will in. He told me that they were there in the hall and that I should go up there and deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what were these telephones that you were using that day? How were I able to communicate with Ismet Sogolj?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a land line up at the line, defence line. We used induction telephones. You ring and then you turn the crank, and three or four telephones can listen into the communication. That was the system that we used to communicate and to arrange things up at the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So having received this telephone call, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he notified me that there were prisoners, I, as the assistant commander for security, was duty bound to go and take in those prisoners and then to transfer them further on. First of all, I went to check what was actually there because I didn't know that. When I descended down to Kesten, I used the road. The most difficult part was moving through the area between our lines and the enemy lines because there were minefield there is, but we managed to pass through without walking into any of the mines. I went there to the hall in Kesten. The company commander was waiting for me in front of the hall. He told me there were quite a few prisoners and that I should have a look at them. When I entered the hall, there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Let's take this one stage at a time, Mr. Karahasanovic. First of all, do you remember approximately what time it was during the day that you descended down to Kesten?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in the afternoon. I can't remember now the exact time, but I think it was maybe somewhere between 14 and 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you able to say how long, approximately, it took you to get to Kesten from Malovan Greda?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 20 minutes or so, since of it downhill and it was easier to walk down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did anything happen on the way down to Kesten?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I walked towards Kesten, I encountered a soldier leading three women. I asked him who they were, and he said that they, too, had been captured together with the people who were in the hall. I told him to go down to the command with them and to wait there for us to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Which direction were they going in when you encountered them?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were moving towards Malovan Greda, which means that they were moving from Kesten to Malovan Greda. That was the footpath, a footpath that we could use because it was already made and it was a little bit safer than the other routes, primarily in terms of mine danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You told us earlier in your evidence that the 5th Battalion had a number of command posts or forward command posts. Did you say which location the soldier was to take the three women?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was supposed to take them to Marici because Marici was the closest location where he could wait and there was a path leading to that place; and then on my way back, I was supposed to note down their personal details because the soldiers had done some of that. But then later on when the police would arrive, I was supposed to transfer them on to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, on the map in front of you, do you see Kesten village?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I think I'm right in saying that you mentioned that you saw people. There were people in a hall. Are you able to mark on the map where the hall was?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hall, where the hall was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately, somewhere here. Can I make a circle?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somewhere around this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if could you please mark that circle with the number 4.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what did you find when you got to the hall in Kesten?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I entered the hall, I was able to see a large number of prisoners. The hall may have been maybe 12 metres long and maybe 8 metres wide; and then along the three of the walls, there was nobody at the wall where the door was; but there, along the remaining three walls, that's where the prisoners were lined up. They were facing the wall and they were standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You told us early that Ismet Sogolj had called you from Kesten. Did you see Mr. Sogolj when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was waiting for me in front of the hall. When I entered the hall, Sogolj, since his units was supposed to move on cleaning up the terrain, he said, "This is for you. There are three or four guards in there and they're taking care of the prisoners, and now you should do your job." Then he moved forwards with his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When he Mr. Sogolj moved forward with his unit, how many other members of the ABiH were there with you at the hall in Kesten?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were three or four soldiers inside the hall and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What happened next after you saw the soldiers in the hall?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw the soldiers, I saw that there was a large number of those prisoners, and I knew that I couldn't handle this on my own. So I went to where the communication equipment was, the induction telephone just across the road. I phoned up my commander telling him that we had a large number of prisoners, that we would need assistance, and that we would need some means of transport because you could not move them anywhere on foot. He told me he would report to everyone that he would tell the police, that I should wait up there, and that everything would be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, when you say you spoke to your commander, who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to my commander because he was in charge of that area. He was my immediate superior, the man that I was supposed to report to. I couldn't use this phone to talk -- to report to the brigade, but he was to report to them using other means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what was the name of the commander?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ahmed Sehic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you know where he was at the time when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was at Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you please just spell the surname of your commander?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: S-E-H-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what happened after you spoke to Commander Sehic?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke to him, I knew what I was to do. I was, first, to note down the personal details of those prisoners, since the soldiers of the 2nd Company had disarmed them. All the weapons were out there. They were all soldiers wearing uniforms, either camouflage uniforms or olive drab uniforms. There were no civilians among them. All the documents had already been taken away from them, and they were there in front of the hall. I went into the hall, and I started making a list of all of them, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, and I don't think you've mentioned this, these prisoners were members of which armed force?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the enemy army. They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You said that there were documents in front of the hall. Was there anything else outside of the hall that you saw?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a heap of weapons that had been taken away from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is your next question, Mr. Robson, which army they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I could see you wanted clarification there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You told us they were Serbs. Could you tell us which army they were members of?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian army. Because they were members of the Serbian army, there were all Serbs in that area, and it was quite natural, therefore, that it was the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would that be the VRS or JNA or other parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the army the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also have a question, Mr. Robson, if you don't mind. Sir, you said you took down the names and particulars of these POWs, one by one. How many were there finally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I started making a list and I did that one by one. There were 51 of them on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that all of them that were in the hall were put on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what details did you record exactly from the prisoners? What information did you put on the list?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked them for their first and last names, year of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did each prisoner answer your question and provide you with information?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I approached the prisoners, I did that one by one, they were turned to face me; and when I asked them, "What 's your full name, year of birth, and place of birth," they gave me their answers loud and clear. And if I was unable to hear the last name, I would ask them, "Could you please repeat your last name," and I'm sure 100 percent certain that they gave me accurate information, names, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did anything happen while you were taking information from these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When there were only five or six of them left, a group of Arabs walked in. They were armed. There were maybe 20 of them. They were armed. As soon as they walked in, they started making racket in the hall. I continued with my task, making this list, until I was finished, until all 51 of them were on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, could you repeat how many Arabs walked in?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty or so. I didn't count them. There may have been 18 or 22 of them; but 20, that would be an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you describe the Arabs that you saw?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They all spoke in a foreign language. I think it was Arabic. Because I don't speak any other language apart from Bosnian, I think they spoke Arabic. They were shouting and yelling. They had longish beards. They wore those loose clothes, sandals or boots on their foot. They looked like all kinds of things. But one thing was for sure, they didn't look like soldiers. They were smaller in stature than I am. Maybe they were the same size as Mr. Robson here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you able to describe the type of clothing that they were wore in any more detail?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wore those loose shirts and loose trousers. The shirts were worn outside of the trousers. Some of them may have had camouflage jackets, but then they did not have such trousers. They also had some kind of head gear, some caps on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you notice did any of them have any insignia or markings on their clothing?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice any insignia or markings on any of them; whereas, the army soldiers would have patches on their sleeves with designations of their brigades. They did not have any insignia that would make it possible for one to ascertain where they belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did you know which military unit these Arabs belonged to, if any?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know what unit they belonged to. In our area, we knew that there was a Mujahid unit, that's what the rumour was. We were not aware of any other units being in that area or coming into that area, because all the Arabs that we would see, we considered them to be members of the El Mujahedin Unit because we didn't know if they may have belonged to any other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said they came in shouting and yelling. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I finished making the list, one of them spoke our language, Bosnian language. We were able to communicate. I told him that they should leave the room since the prisoners were ours, and that we would transfer them because we had already reported to our superiors that we would transfer them. Once I made the list, once I gathered up all the documents, that we would do that, and they had nothing -- there was nothing for them to do is there in the hall. They started brandishing their weapons in our direction. It is difficult to describe their behaviour. At any moment, you expect them to open fire. They told me that I and my soldiers should leave that room, that I should go out, that they had liberated this area, that we were out of place here, and that it was not our place to be there. I didn't know what to do at that time. In the meantime, the department commander came to the hall. He may have arrived at the same time when those Arabs walked in. He quarrelled them with some more, telling them that they should leave, that we would deal with the prisoners, and that we would do it properly. They were shouting at him. They told him that he should leave the room together with us, that those prisoners belonged to them, and that they were the only ones that could dispose with those prisoners as they saw fit and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify a few things there. You said that "they" told you to leave. Who was it that spoke and told to you leave the hall?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of those Arabs. He didn't tell us his name. He didn't tell us what unit he belonged to. He simply told us, "Leave this area, leave this room. Those prisoners are ours." Let me repeat what he said. He said that they had liberated that area, that everything in that area belonged to them, and that the BiH army had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You said that the deputy commander arrived. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhamed Omarasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And he was the deputy commander for what unit?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the assistant commander of the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you able to say how members of the 328th Brigade were in and around the hall at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were three or four soldiers in the hall. There was myself and Muhamed Omarasevic came later. There were no troops around the hall, because I said that this company went on to carry out its mission elsewhere. They were supposed to search the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what happened next after you were told to leave the hall?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this shouting and the brandishing of weapons, the weapons being trained at us at prisoners and all that, as an officer, I pondered this thing, what to do, and I concluded that the best thing to do would for me to leave. If I oppose them, I had only three or four of those soldiers with us. I was unarmed, Muhamed was unarmed, and they were all unarm the. If I resorted to force, it would have failed. We would maybe be able to kill two or three of them, but I was sure that they would have killed all of us; and so for the benefit of first myself and also of my soldiers, because I was in charge of their safety and security, I decided to leave this room together with those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karahasanovic, you told us that for the benefit of first yourself and also your soldiers, you left the room. It may be that -- did you mention anything else, any other reason in your answer for leaving the room?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said because of safety and security, that of my security as well as the security of my soldiers. If I protected myself, I thought I would be able to protect the soldiers as well as the prisoners as well. Had I used force, although it would have been impossible with the three or four soldiers I had against the 20 of them, it would have meant that my soldiers would have been killed as well as all of the prisoners. Because of that reason, I decided to leave the room. I realised there was no one there to help us and that we had to do what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what happened when you left the hall?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went outside, and I stopped there with my soldiers and the assistant commander. We discussed it; and perhaps some five minutes later, those who were inside took the prisoners out, two by two, and went towards Krcevine and Sjenokos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you look at the happen in front of us, are you able to draw with an arrow the direction that they went in?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I indicate it on the map, I just wanted to say this: When I came out of the hall, there were some ten other Arabs in front of the building. Now I can indicate it for you, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When the prisoners came out of the hall with the Arabs, what happened to the Arabs that were standing outside of the cal?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them positioned themselves on one side of the prisoners, the others on the other. So they moved on the outside and the prisoners were in pairs between them, and the soldiers that had been outside simply joined the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've pointed the direction that they headed in. Did you see where they went?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not see where they went. There is a clearing around the hall, but it amounts to several metres, then there's the forest. There's also a junction there which can take you to Krcevine and Sjenokos; however, I did not see what direction they took since I remained at the hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just clarify a point here. Sir, you said there were approximately 20 Arabs who arrived there. When you left out the hall, there were another ten outside. Are you saying there was approximately a total of 30 Arabs there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Some 20 were inside the hall; but at that time, I wasn't able to see that there were another dozen outside. When I came outside, I saw that some ten or a dozen of them were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What happened next after the Arabs headed north with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Arabs took the captured towards Kesten, or rather, towards Krcevine and Sjenokos. I don't know which exactly. I informed Ahmed Sehic, my superior, that the prisoners were taken away by force. I told him that our lives were at stake as well and that the prisoners were taken away. He said he would inform his superior level, that is, the brigade level, and that he was to come to Kesten himself. Since by that time the prisoners had already been taken away, the heap of documents of theirs remained in front of the hall. I picked it all up, put it in a plastic bag, and the company clerk collected the weapons, since there was another heap of weapons there. He put it in the building where the telephone was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just to clarify a couple of things. First of all, by what means did the Arabs and the prisoners leave the area? What mode of transport did they use?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what mode of transport they had. As far as I could tell, they left the hall on foot, in pairs; that is, the prisoners were in pairs and on the sides were the Arabs. In one column, there were 25 or 26 of them, and in the other column, another 25; and then on the sides were the Arabs. They left on foot for Krcevine or Sjenokos. That was the direction they took.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Next, you told us that you spoke to Ahmed Sehic. By what means did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the phone, the induction phone. The land line was the only one we had. I called him and I told him what I told you a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: After collecting the documents, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the company clerk noted down the serial numbers of weapon, I merely counted the weapons: This many light machine-guns, this many automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, as well as M48s. I simply noted down the number of pieces for the sake of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Witness, could you be a little bit more specific please as regards the direction which the Arabs took together with the prisoners, because on page 24, line 22, you said that they went in the direction of or crossed Krcevine. They passed through that town. Then on page 25 line 15, and on the following pages, you said that you don't know in which direction they left. Then a little further, you said - just a minute - on page 26, line 23, you said that "they went in the direction of," and the name has not been recorded on the transcript. I find this a little bit confusions as far as which direction they went into is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a hall. The hall was in Kesten; and as you leave the hall, there is only one road taking you to Sjenokos and Krcevine. However, in the forest, not too far from the hall, there is a cross-roads which can take you to Krcevine or to Sjenokos. I don't know which direction they took; however, I know that that was the general direction they left. I don't know which turn they took, though. I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karahasanovic, just so we're clear, please could you spell Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Now things are much clearer as far as I'm concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K-R-C-E-V-I-N-A --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: E.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And could you please spell Sjenokos for us?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: S-J-E-N-O-K-O-S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a junction in the forest. Do you see that notice map; and if so, could you put a circle around it?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it. It is here, next to the arrow, the tip of the arrow. That's where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And could you put a number 5 above that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what happened after you collected the ID documents? What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I made a list of the seized weapons for our records, so that I could report that to the brigade. I wrote down how many pieces there were of automatic rifles, light machine-guns, and so on and so forth. There were also semi-automatic rifles and M48s. I simply noted down the quantity of each type of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I should ask you, do you know approximately what time it was when the Arabs headed off with the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was there between 2.00 and 3.00. By the time I made the list, well, I don't think they left before 4.00 p.m. from the Kesten hall in the direction I indicated. 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time. Could I, first of all, please ask that this map be admitted into evidence, and then we can take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will become Exhibit number 1352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take the break at come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Karahasanovic, you were telling us about events on the 10th of September, 1995. Did there come a time when you left Kesten?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Kesten in the evening. When it began getting dark, that's when I left Kesten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Via Malovan Greda to Marici. I knew that the three women were supposed to be there. I was supposed to go down there and get their information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did you see the three women there?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I arrived in Marici, the women were not there; however, the soldier that was with them was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you speak to the soldier?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I asked him where the women were. He was terrified and pale and said, I'm conveying to you now what he told me, that a van came along with some Arabs. They stopped next to him when he was already in Marici close to the command post. They came out of the van and asked him who the women were. He said that they had been captured with a group of Serb soldiers. As he told me, they also shouted at him, threatened him, and took the women away. They put them in the van and drove off. He remained alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately what time was it during the day that you saw the soldier and the three women as you travelled from Malovan Greda to Kesten?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was between 2.00 and 3.00, during which time I was descending.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did the soldier tell you where he was when the Arabs arrived and took the three women?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in Marici, on the road there, close to our forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you able to say how long approximately it should have taken him and the three women to travel from the point where you met him to get to the road at Marici?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point where we met, it would be some 35 minutes, 30 to 35 minutes, to get down to Marici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Where did you go to next?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the bag with the documents with me. Everyone by that time knew of what had taken place that day, and I left for Polje with a vehicle from Marici. It was a difficult day for me and I needed rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: After leaving Kesten, did you see the prisoners of war again at any stage?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we left the hall, I never saw the prisoners again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you wrote the names of all the Serb prisoners of war on a piece of paper. At this stage if I could please show you Exhibit 646, and if you can look at the document on the left-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can please go to the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document at all?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the list I drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This list we see in front of us, when did you prepare it?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th. The report was sent on the 11th. When I was at the Kesten hall, I wasn't able to spell this nicely. So this is actually a copied version of the 18th, so that I could leave it with the commander and send a written report to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That answer was not clear at all, Mr. Karahasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was clear. What's unclear about the answer, sir? No, the date is the 18th. He can --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You said: "When I was at Kesten hall, I wasn't able to spell this nicely. So this is actually a copied version of the 18th." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Robson. He means the 18th. I think that's not a correct question to put the witness. I think this document is dated the 11th. He says he redid the list on the 10th. Now he is talking of a document of the 18th. He must explain the discrepancy. To say to what does he mean by that. He means the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you just -- let me ask that question again, please, if I may. Can you just explain for us what this document is that we see in front of us and how you prepared it?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my report that I drafted on the 11th, so that there would be a written trace for the commander. The report was sent to the brigade. That was the 11th of September, 1995; that is when I wrote the report. I had to copy the original list since I couldn't send the report I sent -- I wrote on the 10th. I copied it on the 11th, the next day, so that I could send it to the brigade command, so that it could be archived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, what did you with the list that you drew on the 10th, from which you copied this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I no longer needed the document since I copied it legibly. I kept one original and sent another to the commander and the brigade. The old, the previous one, to me was unimportant. I discarded of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can just look at the three pages in sequence. We're looking at page number 1. If we can look at page number 2, and if we go back to the first page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to see that page?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can look at the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is all of the writing that we see on this document your writing?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us which writing we see in this document does not belong to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can start with page number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 1, when it says "1300," that's not my handwriting. Everything else is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at page number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 2, this is all my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then if we can move to the final page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, down to 51, that is my handwriting. My handwriting is also: 4 Arabs, 3 women, 2 killed, 2 children released. That is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote the other words that we can see in this document?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know who had access to the documents so as to be able to write this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can ask you about the words that you wrote underneath the names of the men, where it says "4 Arabs," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that morning, when I talked to the company commander, he told me that that morning another four members of the Serb army had been captured, I wrote "4 Arapi." I thought I would be the only one to use the document and that the people at the brigade would understand the meaning. In the report I forwarded subsequently, I expanded the note, but this was merely to be added on to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we understand that the four BH army soldiers who were captured were Arabs -- sorry, members of the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Four soldiers that were captured by the Arabs were from the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, wait. I don't understand you, sir. In your answer, at page 34, you said: "That morning, when I talked to the company commander, he told me that that morning another four members of the Serb army had been captured, and I wrote '4 Arapi.' I thought I would be the only one to use the document." Why did you write "4 Arapi"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just so that I knew that four had been captured by Arabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have I understood you well? You said that four Serb soldiers were captured and taken away instantly by the Arabs, in addition to the 51 members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These four before a list is made of the 51, because this is what happened -- that happened in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, they were captured where they were found and then taken away by the Arabs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't know where they had captured them. I didn't see that. I just received this information from the company commander that four of them had been captured in the morning there in the Kesten area, and that they were taken away by the Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can move on to the next item we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Why did you write "3 women"?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because three women were also captured and I did not list their names. I didn't know their names, so I merely noted down that three women will also been captured. As I explained, they had been taken away by the Arabs. I didn't have their names, the names of these women to put them down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't written "Arapi" next to them, but you are telling us that they were taken by Arabs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I didn't. I merely noted that three women had been captured on that day. That's what I noted in my report about those three women who had been captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us with respect to the men you write they were taken by Arabs, and with respect to the women you don't; and yet today, you are telling us that the women were taken by the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because the company commander had told me that four had been captured by the Arabs and that had been taken away immediately. The three women, as I've already noted, that was the report that I merely sent to my commander and to the brigade. The supplemental report that I drafted contained additional explanations to the effect that those women were captured by the Arabs and that they had been forcefully taken away from us, as had been the 51 prisoners. So I provided more details in my report, and these are just the names and just some bullet points explaining what happened. I didn't go into any detailed explanations for each item. I just jotted down the individual items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. You're telling us today that these three women were also taken by the Arabs. You found it appropriate to write "4 Arapi," and you're telling us that by that you mean that four POWs were taken by Arabs. Now, you're also telling us today that the three women were also taken by Arabs, but you're not also writing "Arapi" next to them in. I just want you -- I understand that these were just short notes, bullet points, but how then do you remember that these three women were taken by Arabs if you don't write "Arapi" next to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do remember the events that happened. I remember everything that happened on that day. It is still in my memory, because that day was the day when 51 prisoners were taken away from us forcefully by force. Three women were taken by force. It all happened on that day, and it is not very easier for one to actually forget that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Arabs that took the three women were members of the same group of Arabs that you saw take the men from Kesten?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. But it couldn't have been the same group, because that must have happened at the same time when those people had come to the hall, and that other lad leading the three women was taking those women down that there at the same time. So it couldn't have been the same group that was in the hall at the same time as the three women were being taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Returning to the list, you wrote the words "2 killed." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The company commander also relayed to me that two Serb soldiers had been killed when the 51 and those two surrendered. The thing that happened was probably that they regretted having done that, and they tried to seize the rifle from one of the soldiers that was escorting them towards the hall; and, as a result, they were killed by our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You said: "The thing that happened was probably that they regretted having done that ..." Who is the "they" that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those Serb prisoners, because when I said that they had tried to seize the weapons, two of our soldiers were wounded in the struggle about weapons; and quite naturally, the others opened fire, killing those two men who had tried to seize the weapons from our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just so we're absolutely clear, when you say that "they were killed by our soldiers," who do you mean by "our soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers of the BH army, from the 2nd Company, Ismet Sogolj's company. He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then the last thing that you wrote on this list was "2 children." Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two children, this is again what you heard from the company commander in this conversation. He told me that they were two underage children with the prisoners and that they had let those children go. I don't know where those children had gone to, because I simply didn't hear anything about that. They released them, they were alive and well when they were let go, and I think they did it so as to prevent them being imprisoned with the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you see the children?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, if we can please go back to the first page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you wrote this document and I'd just like to have a look at a few of the names that you wrote down. At number one, we can see the name Nedzo Jovic; at number 2, we can see the name Nenad Gligoric; number 3, it says Slavko Todorovic; and then at number 7, can you read out the name there, please?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cupeljic Mirko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then if we look at the third page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you read out the name at number 51 for us, please?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cupeljic, M, Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you could please bear those names in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours at this stage we can put this document away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just go back to the first Cupeljic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could please bring up on the screen in front of us, it is Exhibit 651, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karahasanovic, this is a letter from the Bosnia and Herzegovina Ministry of Defence to the Office of the Prosecutor dated 19th of April, 2006. It encloses a report from the Chief of Staff of the Republika Srpska army. Did you have a chance to see this document during the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, had you ever seen this document before coming to The Hague just a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you the report from the Chief of Staff of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It is at page 3 in the English version; and in the B/C/S version, it is the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago, we looked at some of the names contained on your list. And if we could look at the names we find here, could you read the first three names to us?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovic Nedzo, son of Milan; Gligorovic Nenad, son of Bozo, Todorovic Savo, son of Djordje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then at entry number 7 on the list, what name is there?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cupeljic Mirko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now you had the opportunity to look at this document. Do you have any comments upon the names that we see on the list in front of us?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that the names are the name as the ones that I listed with some minor differences, and I can see that the places of birth are not the same on this list. But the year of birth and the names are the same with the exception of Savo Todorovic. I think it said "Slavko," and it says "Savo" here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So with the exception of some minor differences, the 51 names contained on this list and the 51 names contained on your list are the same?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And are the names listed in the same order or the same sequence as we find them on your list?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And on your list, at entry number 7 and entry number 51, you read out the names of those persons, and they both had the name -- the surname Cupeljic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we look at entry 51 on this list, please. It's the last page in both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you read out the name at entry 51?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maric Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So is this a different name to the entry 51 on your list?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a different name. I don't think that I have this name on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can look at the first sentence in the following paragraph, what it says is: "According to the RS army General Staff reports, under ordinal number 7 and 51 of the list attached to the request, the same person is the case." So that sentence suggests a list was attached to a request which was sent to the Bosnian authorities, and it says "the same person is the case." According to your list, is there any risk that you made a mistake and repeated the details of the same person at entry number 7 and 52?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible that I might have made such a mistake, because the first Cupeljic, I think, was born in 1945, as far as I could recall, at the six kilometre; and the second one listed under 51 on my list is 20 years his junior. So it could not have happened that I made such a mistake to confuse the two men of that kind, especially since I knew there was another Cupeljic. So I wrote the initial of his father there, indicating that there are two people with the same last names and that these are two different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it might be usual just to go back to the first list just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go back to that first list, I don't know what the witness said. I see the transcript says that one Cupeljic was born "1945." It was "1954," according to his list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your answer a moment ago, you mentioned the year that the first Cupeljic was born. Can you remember what year that was that? What year did you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to his list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can bring back Exhibit 646, please, and if we can look at page number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So can we see here the first Cupeljic that you took details from?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cupeljic. Yes, well, I did not remember the exact year. It says "1954," but I said that the age difference between the two was 20 years. This other man was born there 1975, this one is born there 1954, so that would be 20 years or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The first was Mirko Cupeljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3, please, at entry 51.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we see the capital "M" in brackets after the surname Cupeljic there. Why did you write that?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've just explained, since there was another Cupeljic already, I took the initial of his father's name and I put it in brackets, and then went on to write his name just to indicate that this is not one and the name person. I have already explained that it was impossible for them to be one person because there was this age difference of some 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can return back to Exhibit 651, MFI, please. Your Honours, at this stage, I would move that we admit Exhibit 651, MFI, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was marked for identification before we objected to its admissibility based on a lack of foundation that had been laid. Although the witness is able to comment that the names appear to be the same on two documents, that is something that Your Honours can also see, but there is other information contained in this document that the witness is not able to -- to discuss. He didn't author the document, he didn't receive the document, he doesn't know anything about how this document was put together. There is, as you know, mention in there about exhumation. There is no showing at all that this person participated in any exhumations. And if the document goes into evidence, it goes into evidence in whole, and there's no foundation laid through this witness about the details that are contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, you've heard today how Mr. Karahasanovic took a list from -- from 51 men in very difficult circumstances. Those men are the subject of this indictment. It obviously goes to matters of key importance in this case. Here, on the screen in front of us, we have a document from some 11 years later, which purports to give information and details about those very same 51 men with some minor exceptions. There is no way that this list in front of us could have been generated by chance or coincidence. We have heard how the names are the same, save for those slight differences. The names are sequentially in the same order as Mr. Karahasanovic's list. Mr. Karahasanovic has been able to comment on the substance of the document. This Trial Chamber obviously requires a link between the witness and the document in order to admit it. It is my submission that this witness is not merely read out the list, he has been able to comment upon it and deal with the substance of the document. That being the case, Your Honours, I would submit that you could and should admit it. And as to the question as to what wealth to attach to this document, that is a matter that can you leave to your discretion at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
